script.opening: "Doc, this came on suddenly in my left side and it’s agony — it comes in waves and shoots down towards my groin. I literally can’t keep still, I’m pacing. I feel sick, and I think there was blood in my wee. I’ve never had anything like it."

facts.text: Started about 3 hours ago, at work, suddenly. Left side of the back below the ribs, comes in waves every few minutes, shoots down into the left groin and the top of the left testicle. "10 out of 10 at its worst." Pacing around; can’t sit still. Moving doesn’t make it worse.

Vomited twice; can’t keep water down. Urine looked "pinkish" an hour ago; going more often, no burning. No fever, no shivers, "I don’t think I’m hot". Not faint or dizzy. No diarrhoea. Testicle itself not swollen.
No back injury. No chest pain, no breathlessness. Pain doesn’t go into the middle of the tummy or through to the back in the middle. Has two kidneys as far as he knows; no kidney problems before.
Fit and well. No medicines, no allergies. No asthma, no stomach ulcers, no heart or kidney problems. Took two paracetamol an hour ago — no help.
Roofer — works outside, "doesn’t drink much water, mostly tea and energy drinks". Drinks 15 units a week, smokes 10 a day. Lives with his partner, Siobhan, who is at home and has a car.
Dad had kidney stones "a couple of times".

In obvious pain: shift around, wince, pause mid-sentence as a wave comes. Answer briefly. You want the pain stopped. If told to go to hospital, ask "Can’t I just have something at home?" and accept if it is explained. Ask what it is if the doctor doesn’t say.

ice.ideas: "My dad had kidney stones — is that what this is?"
ice.concerns: "The blood scared me. I just want the pain to stop." Worried about missing work — he’s self-employed with a job to finish.
ice.expectations: "Something for the pain, now, and to know what it is."

cues: "I can’t keep still, I’m pacing" — restlessness typical of colic.
"I think there was blood in my wee" — fear to address and a supporting sign.
"Can’t I just have something at home?" — negotiate same-day assessment and safe transport (not driving).

checkpoints.text: Recognises RENAL/URETERIC COLIC (sudden colicky loin-to-groin pain in waves, RESTLESS/unable to keep still — unlike peritonitis, haematuria, nausea) as the likely diagnosis

Provides prompt effective ANALGESIA — NSAID by any route first-line (e.g. diclofenac PR/IM at a face-to-face assessment) unless contraindicated (MHRA June 2013 diclofenac CV contraindications), IV paracetamol next, opioid only if both are contraindicated or insufficient (NICE NG118), antiemetic — not under-treating severe pain

EXCLUDES the dangerous mimics — above all a leaking/ruptured ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM (especially older/vascular patients), an infected obstructed kidney (urosepsis), ectopic pregnancy, and other acute-abdomen causes — rather than anchoring on "stone"
Investigates appropriately — urine dip, urgent LOW-DOSE NON-CONTRAST CT-KUB within 24 hours (imaging of choice, NICE NG118), U&E (AKI), FBC/CRP, pregnancy test in women (ultrasound if pregnant/young)

Recognises ADMISSION/urgent-referral criteria — infection with obstruction (urgent decompression), AKI, single/transplant kidney, uncontrolled pain, large/high stone, dehydration, uncertainty — vs safe outpatient passage of small stones
Responds to severe pain with urgency and empathy, explains the likely diagnosis and plan, and checks understanding
Gives stone advice and recurrence prevention (most small stones pass, hydration, diet, stone analysis/metabolic work-up) where appropriate

Safety-nets robustly: urgent return for FEVER/rigors (infected obstruction), uncontrolled pain, anuria or feeling very unwell; appropriate referral/imaging; review — analgesia + imaging + AAA/sepsis exclusion, not anchoring on "just a stone"

worked.txt: "That pacing-can’t-keep-still pain shooting to the groin, with blood in your urine, really sounds like a kidney stone passing. First priority — let’s get on top of that pain with a strong anti-inflammatory, which works best for this, plus something for the sickness."

"I do need to be thorough rather than just assume a stone — I can’t check your tummy, pulses or blood pressure over video, and with pain and vomiting like this you need to be seen in person today, because some serious things can mimic this, and I’ll ask about fevers."

"I’ll dip your urine and arrange an urgent low-dose CT scan of the kidneys within 24 hours — that’s the best test to confirm a stone, see its size and whether it’s blocking. I’ll also check your kidney function and infection markers."

"If it’s a small stone, no infection and your kidneys are fine, these usually pass at home with pain relief and plenty of fluids. But if you spike a fever, the pain can’t be controlled, or your kidney’s blocked, you’d need hospital — a blocked, infected kidney is an emergency."
"So watch for this: fever or shivering, pain we can’t settle, not passing urine, or feeling really unwell — that’s urgent, ring us or go to A&E. Otherwise drink plenty and we’ll follow up the scan."

"Once it’s passed, we can look at preventing more — staying well hydrated — around 2.5 to 3 litres of water a day — some diet tweaks, and analysing the stone if you catch it. Stones do like to recur, so it’s worth it."

f.learning: Sudden severe COLICKY LOIN pain radiating to the GROIN, in waves, with the patient RESTLESS and unable to get comfortable (a discriminator from peritonitis, where patients lie still), plus nausea/vomiting and HAEMATURIA, is the classic picture of RENAL/URETERIC COLIC from a stone. Provide prompt effective ANALGESIA — an NSAID by any route is first-line (NICE NG118; e.g. diclofenac PR/IM, which needs a face-to-face assessment) unless contraindicated (MHRA June 2013: diclofenac contraindicated in established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease and congestive heart failure), then IV paracetamol, then an opioid only if both are contraindicated or insufficient, plus an antiemetic — as an early priority alongside assessment. Critically, do NOT anchor on "just a stone": exclude the dangerous MIMICS, above all a leaking/ruptured ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM (especially in older or vascular patients presenting with loin/back pain — rapidly fatal, needs emergency vascular assessment), an INFECTED OBSTRUCTED kidney (fever/sepsis with obstruction is a urological emergency needing urgent decompression), ECTOPIC pregnancy (always pregnancy-test women of childbearing age), and other acute-abdomen causes. Investigate with a urine dip (blood supports the diagnosis but its absence does not exclude it) and an urgent LOW-DOSE NON-CONTRAST CT-KUB within 24 hours as the imaging of choice (confirming stone size/site/obstruction), plus U&E (AKI), FBC/CRP, and a pregnancy test (ultrasound if pregnant/young). Recognise admission/urgent-referral criteria — infection with obstruction, AKI, single/transplant kidney, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, large/high stone, dehydration, bilateral obstruction, uncertainty — while small distal stones often pass with analgesia, hydration and follow-up. Safety-net for fever/rigors, uncontrolled pain, anuria or feeling very unwell, and advise on stone passage and recurrence prevention.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG118 Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management (2019) · [2] NICE QS195 Renal and ureteric stones (2020) · [3] NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 and over · [4] MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2013 (diclofenac: new contraindications and warnings) · [5] BNF
knowledge.summary: Classic left ureteric colic in a restless man with haematuria and vomiting. Relieve pain with an NSAID by any route, arrange low-dose non-contrast CT within 24 hours, and ask actively about fever and vascular disease so an infected obstructed kidney or a leaking aneurysm is not missed. Vomiting with uncontrolled pain means he needs same-day hospital assessment.

points.t: Sudden severe colicky loin pain radiating to the groin, restlessness (people with peritonitis lie still), nausea or vomiting and haematuria. A normal urine dip does not exclude a stone. Ask about fever, previous stones, a single or transplanted kidney, and urine output.

NG118 [1]: offer an NSAID by any route as first-line analgesia for suspected renal colic. Offer intravenous paracetamol if NSAIDs are contraindicated or not enough, and consider opioids if both are contraindicated or not enough. Do not offer antispasmodics. Diclofenac is contraindicated in established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease and congestive heart failure [4]; check NSAID cautions in the BNF [5].

NG118 [1]: urgent low-dose non-contrast CT within 24 hours of presentation for adults with suspected renal colic; ultrasound instead in pregnancy, and first-line in children and young people. QS195 [2] sets CT within 24 hours as a quality statement. Check renal function, FBC and CRP.

A leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm can present as loin or back pain, especially in older people with vascular risk factors: think of it with collapse, hypotension or a pulsatile mass. Fever or rigors with an obstructed kidney is a urological emergency needing urgent decompression; assess for sepsis using NG253 [3]. In women, always consider ectopic pregnancy.

Refer when pain is not controlled or vomiting stops oral treatment, with any sign of infection or sepsis, reduced kidney function, a single or transplanted kidney, suspected bilateral obstruction, or diagnostic doubt. Otherwise, many small stones pass with analgesia and follow-up. NG118 [1]: consider an alpha-blocker for distal ureteric stones under 10 mm (off-label).
NG118 [1]: advise adults with stones to drink 2.5 to 3 litres of water a day and keep a normal calcium intake rather than restricting it. Stone analysis guides further prevention.

model.text: Hello Niall, it’s Dr Morgan. I can see you’re in a lot of pain. Tell me what’s happening.

This came on suddenly in my left side and it’s agony. It comes in waves and shoots down to my groin. I can’t keep still, I’m pacing. I feel sick, and I think there was blood in my wee. I’ve never had anything like it.
I’m sorry, that sounds awful. I’ll keep this quick and focused so we can get you pain relief. Is that okay?
model.why: Prioritises; keeps consultation brief and targeted

model.text: Please.
When did it start, and have you been sick?
A few hours ago. I’ve been sick, and I can’t keep anything down.
Have you felt hot or shivery, or had shaking attacks?
No shivers. I don’t think I’m hot.
Are you still passing urine? Any burning?
model.why: Checks urine output and infection symptoms

model.text: Yes, a bit. No burning. It looked pinkish.
Has any doctor told you that you have one kidney, kidney problems, or problems with your heart or circulation? Any asthma or stomach ulcers?
model.why: Single kidney, vascular history, NSAID contraindications

model.text: No, nothing like that that I know of.
Is the pain in your tummy or back as well, or have you felt faint or collapsed at any point?
model.why: Screens for a leaking aneurysm and peritonism

model.text: No, it’s the side and down to the groin. Not faint, just awful.
What have you been thinking this might be?
I wondered if it’s a kidney stone. But the blood scared me. I just want the pain to stop and to know what it is.
That’s understandable. Blood in the urine is common with a stone, but I’ll make sure it gets properly checked.

I think you’re most likely passing a kidney stone down the tube from the kidney to the bladder. The waves of pain, not being able to keep still, and the blood all fit. Other conditions can look similar, and your answers make those less likely, but I can’t examine you on video, so you need to be seen in person.
model.why: Names the likely diagnosis, notes mimics considered and the limits of video

model.text: So what happens now?

The best painkiller for this is an anti-inflammatory, and because you can’t keep tablets down it needs to go in by injection or suppository. You also need a special scan within 24 hours to see the stone and whether it’s blocking the kidney.
model.why: NSAID by non-oral route (NG118) and CT within 24 hours

model.text: Can’t I just have something at home?

Not today, I’m afraid. Because you’re being sick, the pain isn’t controlled, and you need the scan quickly, the safest place is the hospital’s same-day team. They can give strong pain relief, check your kidneys and blood, and do the scan.
model.why: Recognises referral criteria: uncontrolled pain and vomiting

model.text: Okay. That makes sense.
I’ll call the hospital team now and send them my notes. Please don’t drive. Is there someone who can take you straight away? If not, I’ll arrange transport.
I’ll find someone to take me now.
Good. Take a list of any medicines you take, and if you can, collect a urine sample in a clean container.
If before you get there you develop a fever or shivering, the pain moves into your back or tummy and you feel faint, or you collapse, call 999 straight away.
model.why: Specific safety-net for sepsis and aneurysm

model.text: Right.

Many stones pass on their own over a few days to weeks. Once this is over, drinking two and a half to three litres of water a day helps prevent more, and if you catch the stone, we can send it for analysis. Can you tell me what you’re going to do now?
Get someone to take me to hospital now, don’t drive, bring a urine sample, and call 999 if I get a fever or feel faint.
Exactly. I’ll call you tomorrow to see how you got on and what the scan showed.

social.t: He is in severe pain and vomiting. He must not drive; arrange a lift or transport.
Time off while a stone passes may be needed; self-certification covers the first 7 days, then a fit note.

legal.t: A fit note can be issued after 7 days if he is still unfit for work, including by the hospital team.

professional.t: Be honest about what video cannot assess (abdomen, pulses, vital signs). Document the negative answers to fever, collapse and vascular history and the reason for same-day referral.
Check NSAID contraindications and cardiovascular risk before any NSAID (MHRA June 2013 for diclofenac). Opioids are not first-line (NG118).

community.t: Hydration advice (NG118) and stone analysis after passage; community pharmacy can support with analgesia questions.

redFlags: Fever, rigors or feeling very unwell: infected obstructed kidney
Collapse, faintness, back or abdominal pain, especially with vascular risk: leaking aneurysm
Reduced urine output or known single kidney
Vomiting preventing oral analgesia; pain not controlled
psychosocial: Who can take him to hospital
ice: Concern: the blood in his urine
Expectation: pain relief and a diagnosis

playbook.diagnosis: “The pain coming in waves from your side to your groin, not being able to keep still, and blood in the urine fit a kidney stone moving down the tube to the bladder.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A stone is like a small grit trying to squeeze down a narrow straw. Each squeeze of the tube gives a wave of pain. Most small stones get through on their own.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted the pain stopped and to know what it is. Hospital today can do both: proper pain relief and a scan to see the stone.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange a lift, not driving, and a follow-up call.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment: NSAID by injection or suppository, antiemetic
Prevention: 2.5 to 3 litres of water a day; stone analysis
safetyNet: 999 for fever with rigors, faintness, collapse or new back or abdominal pain

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by candidates who anchor on “kidney stone” and send oral tablets. The marks go to screening for the dangerous mimics, choosing the right analgesia route, and arranging CT within 24 hours.

items.fail: No question about fever or rigors.
items.why: An infected obstructed kidney is an emergency needing decompression.
items.fix: Ask directly and put fever in the safety-net.

items.why: It can mimic loin pain and is rapidly fatal, more so in older people with vascular risk.
items.fix: Ask about collapse, faintness, back or abdominal pain and vascular history.

items.fail: Oral analgesia for a vomiting patient, or opioid first.
items.why: NG118: NSAID by any route first-line; the route must work.

items.fail: Routine ultrasound or no imaging plan.
items.why: NG118: low-dose non-contrast CT within 24 hours in adults.
items.fix: Name the scan and the timeframe.
Say what you cannot assess and act on the history.

items.fail: Ignoring his worry about the blood.
items.fix: Acknowledge it and say it will be checked.

avoid.instead: “You can’t keep tablets down, so you need pain relief by injection or suppository and a scan today.”
avoid.why: Oral treatment fails in a vomiting patient, and NG118 makes an NSAID first-line.

avoid.instead: “A stone is most likely. I’ve asked about fever and fainting because other conditions can look similar.”
avoid.why: Anchoring risks missing an infected obstructed kidney or aneurysm.

social.t: He is in severe pain and vomiting. He must not drive; arrange a lift or transport.
Time off while a stone passes may be needed; self-certification covers the first 7 days, then a fit note.

legal.t: A fit note can be issued after 7 days if he is still unfit for work, including by the hospital team.

professional.t: Be honest about what video cannot assess (abdomen, pulses, vital signs). Document the negative answers to fever, collapse and vascular history and the reason for same-day referral.
Check NSAID contraindications and cardiovascular risk before any NSAID (MHRA June 2013 for diclofenac). Opioids are not first-line (NG118).

community.t: Hydration advice (NG118) and stone analysis after passage; community pharmacy can support with analgesia questions.

redFlags: Fever, rigors or feeling very unwell: infected obstructed kidney
Collapse, faintness, back or abdominal pain, especially with vascular risk: leaking aneurysm
Reduced urine output or known single kidney
Vomiting preventing oral analgesia; pain not controlled
psychosocial: Who can take him to hospital
ice: Concern: the blood in his urine
Expectation: pain relief and a diagnosis

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The pain coming in waves from your side to your groin, not being able to keep still, and blood in the urine fit a kidney stone moving down the tube to the bladder.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A stone is like a small grit trying to squeeze down a narrow straw. Each squeeze of the tube gives a wave of pain. Most small stones get through on their own.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted the pain stopped and to know what it is. Hospital today can do both: proper pain relief and a scan to see the stone.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange a lift, not driving, and a follow-up call.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment: NSAID by injection or suppository, antiemetic
Prevention: 2.5 to 3 litres of water a day; stone analysis
safetyNet: 999 for fever with rigors, faintness, collapse or new back or abdominal pain

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by candidates who anchor on “kidney stone” and send oral tablets. The marks go to screening for the dangerous mimics, choosing the right analgesia route, and arranging CT within 24 hours.

items.fail: No question about fever or rigors.
items.why: An infected obstructed kidney is an emergency needing decompression.
items.fix: Ask directly and put fever in the safety-net.

items.why: It can mimic loin pain and is rapidly fatal, more so in older people with vascular risk.
items.fix: Ask about collapse, faintness, back or abdominal pain and vascular history.

items.fail: Oral analgesia for a vomiting patient, or opioid first.
items.why: NG118: NSAID by any route first-line; the route must work.

items.fail: Routine ultrasound or no imaging plan.
items.why: NG118: low-dose non-contrast CT within 24 hours in adults.
items.fix: Name the scan and the timeframe.
Say what you cannot assess and act on the history.

items.fail: Ignoring his worry about the blood.
items.fix: Acknowledge it and say it will be checked.
